IBE-HIBE

2026-07-13 Learning #lattice #ibe #hibe #trapdoors

Notes on IBE and HIBE security games, lattice sampling algorithms, and the trapdoor techniques behind hierarchical encryption.

IBE-HIBE

Security Game (INDr-sID-CPA)

  • Mλ\mathcal{M}_\lambdaMλ​: Message space.
  • Cλ\mathcal{C}_\lambdaCλ​: Ciphertext space.

1. Init

  • The adversary is given the maximum depth of the hierarchy ddd.
  • The adversary outputs a target identity id∗=(I1∗,…,Ik∗)id^* = (I_1^*, \dots, I_k^*)id∗=(I1∗​,…,Ik∗​) where k≤dk \le dk≤d.

2. Setup

  • The challenger runs the algorithm Setup(1λ,1d)\text{Setup}(1^\lambda, 1^d)Setup(1λ,1d) (Note: d=1d = 1d=1 for basic IBE).
  • The challenger gives the Public Parameters ($PP$) to the adversary and keeps the Master Key ($MK$) secret.

3. Phase 1 (Private Key Queries)

  • Queries: The adversary issues queries q1,…,qmq_1, \dots, q_mq1​,…,qm​ to extract private keys for identities idi=(I1,…,Iu)id_i = (I_1, \dots, I_u)idi​=(I1​,…,Iu​) with u≤du \le du≤d.

  • Constraint: idiid_iidi​ must not be a prefix of id∗id^*id∗. This means it cannot be the case that u≤ku \le ku≤k and Ij=Ij∗I_j = I_j^*Ij​=Ij∗​ for all j=1,…,uj = 1, \dots, uj=1,…,u.

  • Response: The challenger runs the Extract algorithm to generate the private key did_idi​ and sends it to the adversary.

  • Note on Adaptivity: These queries can be adaptive, meaning the adversary can analyze previously received keys (from $q_1, \dots, q_{i-1}$) before making the next query.

4. Challenge

  • The adversary outputs a target message M∈MλM \in \mathcal{M}_\lambdaM∈Mλ​.
  • The challenger picks a random bit r∈{0,1}r \in \{0, 1\}r∈{0,1} and a uniformly random ciphertext C∈CλC \in \mathcal{C}_\lambdaC∈Cλ​.
  • If r=0r = 0r=0, the challenge ciphertext is C∗=Encrypt(PP,id∗,M)C^* = \text{Encrypt}(PP, id^*, M)C∗=Encrypt(PP,id∗,M).
  • If r=1r = 1r=1, the challenge ciphertext is C∗=CC^* = CC∗=C.
  • The challenger sends C∗C^*C∗ to the adversary.

5. Phase 2

  • The adversary issues additional adaptive queries qm+1,…,qnq_{m+1}, \dots, q_nqm+1​,…,qn​.
  • The same prefix constraint applies: no queried idiid_iidi​ can be a prefix of id∗id^*id∗.

6. Guess

  • The adversary outputs a guess r′∈{0,1}r' \in \{0, 1\}r′∈{0,1}.
  • The adversary wins the game if r=r′r = r'r=r′

Sampling Algorithms

  • Let A,B∈Zqn×mA, B \in \mathbb{Z}_q^{n \times m}A,B∈Zqn×m​ and R∈{−1,1}m×mR \in \{-1, 1\}^{m \times m}R∈{−1,1}m×m.

  • The construction matrices we work with have the form F=(A∣AR+B)∈Zqn×2mF = (A \mid AR + B) \in \mathbb{Z}_q^{n \times 2m}F=(A∣AR+B)∈Zqn×2m​.

  • Goal: Sample short vectors eee such that F⋅e=u(modq)F \cdot e = u \pmod qF⋅e=u(modq) (i.e., $e \in \Lambda_q^u(F)$).
    We can achieve this using a trapdoor for either the left or right side of FFF:

  • SampleLeft: Uses a trapdoor TAT_ATA​ for Λq⊥(A)\Lambda_q^\bot(A)Λq⊥​(A) to output a short vector eee.

  • SampleRight: Uses a trapdoor TBT_BTB​ for Λq⊥(B)\Lambda_q^\bot(B)Λq⊥​(B) to output a short vector eee.

  • With appropriate parameters, the distributions of eee produced by these two algorithms are statistically indistinguishable.

The Basic IBE Construction

Algorithm TrapGen

TrapGen(q,n)\text{TrapGen}(q,n)TrapGen(q,n) is used to generate a public matrix together with a short trapdoor for its orthogonal lattice.

Inputs:

  • An odd prime modulus q≥3q \ge 3q≥3.
  • A security parameter nnn.
  • The matrix width is usually chosen as m=⌈6nlog⁡q⌉m = \lceil 6n\log q\rceilm=⌈6nlogq⌉.

Outputs:

The algorithm outputs a pair (A,S)(A,S)(A,S), where:

  • A∈Zqn×mA \in \mathbb{Z}_q^{n \times m}A∈Zqn×m​ is the public matrix.
  • S∈Zm×mS \in \mathbb{Z}^{m \times m}S∈Zm×m is a short basis of the lattice Λq⊥(A)\Lambda_q^\bot(A)Λq⊥​(A).

The orthogonal lattice is defined as:

Λq⊥(A)=x∈Zm:Ax=0(modq)\Lambda_q^\bot(A)={x\in \mathbb{Z}^m : Ax = 0 \pmod q}Λq⊥​(A)=x∈Zm:Ax=0(modq)

The generated matrix AAA is statistically close to uniform over Zqn×m\mathbb{Z}_q^{n \times m}Zqn×m​. Therefore, from the public view, AAA looks like a random matrix and does not reveal its trapdoor.

Since SSS is a basis of Λq⊥(A)\Lambda_q^\bot(A)Λq⊥​(A), it satisfies:

AS=0(modq)A S = 0 \pmod qAS=0(modq)

Moreover, SSS is short. With overwhelming probability, its Gram-Schmidt norm is bounded by:

∣S~∣≤O(nlog⁡q)|\widetilde{S}| \le O(\sqrt{n\log q})∣S∣≤O(nlogq​)

The maximum Gram-Schmidt norm produced by TrapGen\text{TrapGen}TrapGen is denoted by σTG\sigma_{TG}σTG​.

Process:

  1. Start from a gadget matrix. The algorithm uses a structured gadget matrix GGG with an efficiently known short trapdoor. This matrix is easy to invert or sample from, but it cannot be used directly as a public matrix because its structure is obvious.

  2. Generate randomness. It samples a random matrix A1A_1A1​ and a small matrix RRR, where the entries of RRR are usually chosen from a small distribution such as −1,0,1{-1,0,1}−1,0,1.

  3. Hide the gadget matrix. The public matrix is constructed by masking the gadget matrix using A1RA_1RA1​R. A simplified form is:

A2=G−A1R(modq),A=[A1∣A2].\begin{aligned} A_2 &= G - A_1R \pmod q, \\ A &= [A_1 \mid A_2]. \end{aligned}A2​A​=G−A1​R(modq),=[A1​∣A2​].​

Then we have:

A[RI]=[A1∣G−A1R][RI]=A1R+(G−A1R)=G(modq).\begin{aligned} A \begin{bmatrix} R\\ I \end{bmatrix} &= [A_1 \mid G - A_1R] \begin{bmatrix} R\\ I \end{bmatrix} \\ &= A_1R + (G - A_1R) \\ &= G \pmod q. \end{aligned}A[RI​]​=[A1​∣G−A1​R][RI​]=A1​R+(G−A1​R)=G(modq).​

This equation shows that knowing RRR allows us to reduce problems involving AAA to problems involving the easy gadget matrix GGG.\

  1. Derive the trapdoor basis.

In the abstract definition of TrapGen\text{TrapGen}TrapGen, the trapdoor is written as a short basis SSS of Λq⊥(A)\Lambda_q^\bot(A)Λq⊥​(A). In the gadget-trapdoor view, the algorithm first obtains a compact trapdoor RRR, and then derives the full basis SSS from RRR and the known short basis of the gadget lattice.

Let BGB_GBG​ be a short basis of Λq⊥(G)\Lambda_q^\bot(G)Λq⊥​(G), so:

GBG=0(modq).G B_G = 0 \pmod q.GBG​=0(modq).

Since:

A[RI]=G(modq),A \begin{bmatrix} R\\ I \end{bmatrix} = G \pmod q,A[RI​]=G(modq),

we can lift every short relation of GGG into a relation of AAA. In particular:

A([RI]BG)=GBG=0(modq).\begin{aligned} A \left( \begin{bmatrix} R\\ I \end{bmatrix} B_G \right) &= G B_G \\ &= 0 \pmod q. \end{aligned}A([RI​]BG​)​=GBG​=0(modq).​

Therefore, the columns of

[RI]BG\begin{bmatrix} R\\ I \end{bmatrix} B_G[RI​]BG​

are short vectors in Λq⊥(A)\Lambda_q^\bot(A)Λq⊥​(A).

However, these vectors only explain how the compact trapdoor RRR gives short relations for AAA. To obtain the full trapdoor basis, the algorithm applies a basis-extension procedure:

S=BasisFromTrapdoor(A,R,BG).S = \textsf{BasisFromTrapdoor}(A,R,B_G).S=BasisFromTrapdoor(A,R,BG​).

The resulting matrix SSS is a full-rank short basis of Λq⊥(A)\Lambda_q^\bot(A)Λq⊥​(A) and satisfies:

AS=0(modq).AS = 0 \pmod q.AS=0(modq).

The important point is that SSS is not sampled randomly. It is derived from the compact trapdoor RRR and the short gadget basis BGB_GBG​. Since both components have small norm, the resulting basis SSS also has bounded Gram-Schmidt norm.

In summary, TrapGen\text{TrapGen}TrapGen creates a public matrix AAA that is statistically close to uniform, while secretly keeping a compact trapdoor RRR. From this trapdoor, one can derive a short basis SSS for Λq⊥(A)\Lambda_q^\bot(A)Λq⊥​(A). This hidden structure is later used in Gaussian sampling algorithms such as SampleLeft\text{SampleLeft}SampleLeft, SampleRight\text{SampleRight}SampleRight, and key extraction.

5. Correctness

We prove that decryption recovers the bit b∈{0,1}b \in \{0,1\}b∈{0,1} correctly with overwhelming probability.

From Extract, the private key SKid=eSK_{id}=eSKid​=e satisfies:

Fide=u(modq)F_{id}e = u \pmod qFid​e=u(modq)

where:

Fid=(A0∣A1+H(id)B)F_{id} = (A_0 \mid A_1 + H(id)B)Fid​=(A0​∣A1​+H(id)B)

During encryption, we have:

c0=uTs+x+b⌊q2⌋(modq)c_0 = u^Ts + x + b\left\lfloor \frac q2 \right\rfloor \pmod qc0​=uTs+x+b⌊2q​⌋(modq)

and

c1=FidTs+[yz](modq)c_1 = F_{id}^Ts + \begin{bmatrix} y \\ z \end{bmatrix} \pmod qc1​=FidT​s+[yz​](modq)

where z=RTyz = R^Tyz=RTy.

In decryption, we compute:

w=c0−eTc1(modq)w = c_0 - e^Tc_1 \pmod qw=c0​−eTc1​(modq)

Substituting c0c_0c0​ and c1c_1c1​ gives:

w=uTs+x+b⌊q2⌋−eT(FidTs+[yz])(modq)=uTs+x+b⌊q2⌋−(Fide)Ts−eT[yz](modq)\begin{aligned} w &= u^Ts + x + b\left\lfloor \frac q2 \right\rfloor - e^T\left(F_{id}^Ts + \begin{bmatrix} y \\ z \end{bmatrix} \right) \pmod q \\ &= u^Ts + x + b\left\lfloor \frac q2 \right\rfloor - (F_{id}e)^Ts - e^T \begin{bmatrix} y \\ z \end{bmatrix} \pmod q \end{aligned}w​=uTs+x+b⌊2q​⌋−eT(FidT​s+[yz​])(modq)=uTs+x+b⌊2q​⌋−(Fid​e)Ts−eT[yz​](modq)​

Since Fide=u(modq)F_{id}e = u \pmod qFid​e=u(modq), we have:

(Fide)Ts=uTs(modq)(F_{id}e)^Ts = u^Ts \pmod q(Fid​e)Ts=uTs(modq)

Therefore:

w=b⌊q2⌋+x−eT[yz](modq)w = b\left\lfloor \frac q2 \right\rfloor + x - e^T \begin{bmatrix} y \\ z \end{bmatrix} \pmod qw=b⌊2q​⌋+x−eT[yz​](modq)

Define the error term as:

err=x−eT[yz]\text{err} = x - e^T \begin{bmatrix} y \\ z \end{bmatrix}err=x−eT[yz​]

Hence:

w=b⌊q2⌋+err(modq)w = b\left\lfloor \frac q2 \right\rfloor + \text{err} \pmod qw=b⌊2q​⌋+err(modq)

So if err\text{err}err is small, then www is close to 000 when b=0b=0b=0, and close to ⌊q/2⌋\left\lfloor q/2 \right\rfloor⌊q/2⌋ when b=1b=1b=1.

Error Bound

Write:

e=(e1∣e2)e = (e_1 \mid e_2)e=(e1​∣e2​)

where e1,e2∈Zme_1,e_2 \in \mathbb{Z}^me1​,e2​∈Zm.

Then:

err=x−e1Ty−e2Tz=x−e1Ty−e2TRTy=x−(e1+Re2)Ty\begin{aligned} \text{err} &= x - e_1^Ty - e_2^Tz \\ &= x - e_1^Ty - e_2^TR^Ty \\ &= x - (e_1 + Re_2)^Ty \end{aligned}err​=x−e1T​y−e2T​z=x−e1T​y−e2T​RTy=x−(e1​+Re2​)Ty​

Since eee is sampled from a discrete Gaussian with parameter σ\sigmaσ, by Lemma 8:

∥e∥≤σ2m\|e\| \le \sigma \sqrt{2m}∥e∥≤σ2m​

with overwhelming probability.

Also, since R←{−1,1}m×mR \leftarrow \{-1,1\}^{m \times m}R←{−1,1}m×m, by Lemma 15:

∥R∥≤O(m)\|R\| \le O(\sqrt m)∥R∥≤O(m​)

with overwhelming probability.

Therefore:

∥e1+Re2∥≤∥e1∥+∥R∥∥e2∥≤O(σm)\|e_1 + Re_2\| \le \|e_1\| + \|R\|\|e_2\| \le O(\sigma m)∥e1​+Re2​∥≤∥e1​∥+∥R∥∥e2​∥≤O(σm)

By Lemma 12, for y←Ψˉαmy \leftarrow \bar{\Psi}_\alpha^my←Ψˉαm​:

∣(e1+Re2)Ty∣≤qσmαω(log⁡m)+O(σm3/2)|(e_1 + Re_2)^Ty| \le q\sigma m\alpha \omega(\sqrt{\log m}) + O(\sigma m^{3/2})∣(e1​+Re2​)Ty∣≤qσmαω(logm​)+O(σm3/2)

Thus, the total error is bounded by:

∣err∣≤qσmαω(log⁡m)+O(σm3/2)|\text{err}| \le q\sigma m\alpha \omega(\sqrt{\log m}) + O(\sigma m^{3/2})∣err∣≤qσmαω(logm​)+O(σm3/2)

with overwhelming probability.

Correct Decryption Condition

For correct decryption, the error must be small enough so that www remains closer to the correct region.

The decryption rule is:

∣w−⌊q2⌋∣<⌊q4⌋\left|w - \left\lfloor \frac q2 \right\rfloor\right| < \left\lfloor \frac q4 \right\rfloor​w−⌊2q​⌋​<⌊4q​⌋

If this holds, output 1$; otherwise, output $0.

It is sufficient to require:

∣err∣<q5|\text{err}| < \frac q5∣err∣<5q​

Therefore, we need:

qσmαω(log⁡m)+O(σm3/2)<q5q\sigma m\alpha \omega(\sqrt{\log m}) + O(\sigma m^{3/2}) < \frac q5qσmαω(logm​)+O(σm3/2)<5q​

This is satisfied when:

α<1σmω(log⁡m)\alpha < \frac{1}{\sigma m\omega(\sqrt{\log m})}α<σmω(logm​)1​

and

q=Ω(σm3/2)q = \Omega(\sigma m^{3/2})q=Ω(σm3/2)

Parameter Choice

The paper chooses the following parameters:

m=6n1+δm = 6n^{1+\delta}m=6n1+δ q=m2.5⋅ω(log⁡n)q = m^{2.5}\cdot \omega(\sqrt{\log n})q=m2.5⋅ω(logn​) σ=m⋅ω(log⁡n)\sigma = m\cdot \omega(\sqrt{\log n})σ=m⋅ω(logn​) α=[m2⋅ω(log⁡n)]−1\alpha = \left[ m^2\cdot \omega(\sqrt{\log n}) \right]^{-1}α=[m2⋅ω(logn​)]−1

where nnn is the security parameter.

These parameters ensure that:

∣err∣<q5|\text{err}| < \frac q5∣err∣<5q​

with overwhelming probability.

Therefore, decryption outputs the correct bit bbb with overwhelming probability.

Security Games for Basic IBE

Security Model

Basic IBE is proven secure in the INDr-sID-CPA model. This is a selective-ID model, so the adversary must announce the target identity id∗id^*id∗ before seeing the public parameters.

The challenger then gives either a real encryption of the challenge bit or a uniformly random ciphertext from the ciphertext space. The adversary's goal is to distinguish which case it received.

Game 0: The Real Security Game

Game 0 is the original INDr-sID-CPA game for Basic IBE.

The public parameters are:

PP=(A0,A1,B,u)PP=(A_0,A_1,B,u)PP=(A0​,A1​,B,u)

Here A0A_0A0​ is generated by TrapGen\text{TrapGen}TrapGen, so the challenger knows the trapdoor TA0T_{A_0}TA0​​ for Λq⊥(A0)\Lambda_q^\bot(A_0)Λq⊥​(A0​). The matrices A1A_1A1​ and BBB are uniform random matrices.

For a private-key query id≠id∗id \neq id^*id=id∗, the challenger computes:

Fid=(A0∣A1+H(id)B)F_{id}=(A_0 \mid A_1+H(id)B)Fid​=(A0​∣A1​+H(id)B)

and answers using:

e←SampleLeft(A0,A1+H(id)B,TA0,u,σ)e \leftarrow \text{SampleLeft}(A_0,A_1+H(id)B,T_{A_0},u,\sigma)e←SampleLeft(A0​,A1​+H(id)B,TA0​​,u,σ)

This is exactly the real key extraction algorithm.

Game 1: Programming the Target Identity

Game 1 changes only the way A1A_1A1​ is generated. The challenger chooses a small random matrix:

R∗←{−1,1}m×mR^* \leftarrow \{-1,1\}^{m\times m}R∗←{−1,1}m×m

and sets:

A1=A0R∗−H(id∗)BA_1 = A_0R^* - H(id^*)BA1​=A0​R∗−H(id∗)B

For the target identity id∗id^*id∗, we get:

A1+H(id∗)B=A0R∗−H(id∗)B+H(id∗)B=A0R∗.\begin{aligned} A_1+H(id^*)B &= A_0R^* - H(id^*)B + H(id^*)B \\ &= A_0R^*. \end{aligned}A1​+H(id∗)B​=A0​R∗−H(id∗)B+H(id∗)B=A0​R∗.​

Therefore:

Fid∗=(A0∣A0R∗)F_{id^*}=(A_0 \mid A_0R^*)Fid∗​=(A0​∣A0​R∗)

This special form is useful because it lets the simulator embed the LWE challenge into the target ciphertext.

Game 0 and Game 1 are statistically close. Intuitively, A0R∗A_0R^*A0​R∗ is statistically close to a uniform matrix, so A1A_1A1​ still looks random. In the ABB proof, the same randomness-extraction argument also handles the leakage of (R∗)Ty(R^*)^Ty(R∗)Ty used in the challenge ciphertext.

Game 2: Switching the Trapdoor to BBB

Game 2 changes how the public matrices are generated. Now A0A_0A0​ is chosen as a random matrix, while BBB is generated using TrapGen\text{TrapGen}TrapGen. Therefore, the challenger knows the trapdoor TBT_BTB​ instead of TA0T_{A_0}TA0​​.

The matrix A1A_1A1​ is still programmed as:

A1=A0R∗−H(id∗)BA_1 = A_0R^* - H(id^*)BA1​=A0​R∗−H(id∗)B

For a private-key query id≠id∗id \neq id^*id=id∗, we expand:

Fid=(A0∣A1+H(id)B)=(A0∣A0R∗−H(id∗)B+H(id)B)=(A0∣A0R∗+(H(id)−H(id∗))B).\begin{aligned} F_{id} &=(A_0 \mid A_1+H(id)B) \\ &=(A_0 \mid A_0R^* - H(id^*)B + H(id)B) \\ &=(A_0 \mid A_0R^* + (H(id)-H(id^*))B). \end{aligned}Fid​​=(A0​∣A1​+H(id)B)=(A0​∣A0​R∗−H(id∗)B+H(id)B)=(A0​∣A0​R∗+(H(id)−H(id∗))B).​

Because HHH is an FRD map, for id≠id∗id \neq id^*id=id∗, the matrix H(id)−H(id∗)H(id)-H(id^*)H(id)−H(id∗) is full-rank. Thus TBT_BTB​ also works as a trapdoor for (H(id)−H(id∗))B(H(id)-H(id^*))B(H(id)−H(id∗))B.

The challenger can answer the key query using:

e←SampleRight(A0,(H(id)−H(id∗))B,R∗,TB,u,σ)e \leftarrow \text{SampleRight} \left( A_0, (H(id)-H(id^*))B, R^*, T_B, u, \sigma \right)e←SampleRight(A0​,(H(id)−H(id∗))B,R∗,TB​,u,σ)

The output eee is distributed statistically close to a valid secret key for ididid.

The challenger cannot answer a key query for id∗id^*id∗, because then:

H(id)−H(id∗)=0H(id)-H(id^*)=0H(id)−H(id∗)=0

and the right-side trapdoor disappears. This is allowed because the selective-ID security game forbids the adversary from asking for the private key of the target identity.

Game 3: Random Challenge Ciphertext

Game 3 is the same as Game 2, except that the challenge ciphertext is replaced by a uniformly random element of the ciphertext space:

CT∗←Zq×Zq2mCT^* \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_q \times \mathbb{Z}_q^{2m}CT∗←Zq​×Zq2m​

Since the challenge ciphertext is random and independent of the challenge bit, the adversary has zero advantage in this game.

Reduction from LWE

The difference between Game 2 and Game 3 is bounded by the hardness of LWE.

The simulator receives LWE samples:

(ui,vi)(u_i,v_i)(ui​,vi​)

It uses the vectors u1,…,umu_1,\dots,u_mu1​,…,um​ to form A0A_0A0​:

A0=[u1∣⋯∣um]A_0=[u_1|\cdots|u_m]A0​=[u1​∣⋯∣um​]

and uses u0u_0u0​ as the public vector uuu.

For the challenge ciphertext, let:

v∗=(v1,…,vm)Tv^*=(v_1,\dots,v_m)^Tv∗=(v1​,…,vm​)T

The simulator sets:

c0∗=v0+b∗⌊q2⌋c_0^* = v_0 + b^*\left\lfloor \frac{q}{2} \right\rfloorc0∗​=v0​+b∗⌊2q​⌋

and:

c1∗=[v∗(R∗)Tv∗]c_1^* = \begin{bmatrix} v^*\\ (R^*)^T v^* \end{bmatrix}c1∗​=[v∗(R∗)Tv∗​]

If the oracle is an LWE oracle, then:

v∗=A0Ts+yv^*=A_0^Ts+yv∗=A0T​s+y

and therefore:

c1∗=[A0Ts+y(R∗)T(A0Ts+y)]=[A0Ts+y(A0R∗)Ts+(R∗)Ty]=(Fid∗)Ts+[y(R∗)Ty].\begin{aligned} c_1^* &= \begin{bmatrix} A_0^Ts+y\\ (R^*)^T(A_0^Ts+y) \end{bmatrix} \\ &= \begin{bmatrix} A_0^Ts+y\\ (A_0R^*)^Ts+(R^*)^Ty \end{bmatrix} \\ &= (F_{id^*})^Ts+ \begin{bmatrix} y\\ (R^*)^Ty \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned}c1∗​​=[A0T​s+y(R∗)T(A0T​s+y)​]=[A0T​s+y(A0​R∗)Ts+(R∗)Ty​]=(Fid∗​)Ts+[y(R∗)Ty​].​

This is distributed as a real challenge ciphertext in Game 2. Also, v0=uTs+xv_0=u^Ts+xv0​=uTs+x, so:

c0∗=uTs+x+b∗⌊q2⌋c_0^*=u^Ts+x+b^*\left\lfloor \frac{q}{2} \right\rfloorc0∗​=uTs+x+b∗⌊2q​⌋

which matches the real encryption form.

If the oracle is random, then v0v_0v0​ and v∗v^*v∗ are random. By the same randomness-extraction argument used above, the pair visible in c1∗c_1^*c1∗​ is statistically close to uniform, so the challenge ciphertext is distributed as in Game 3.

Therefore, any adversary that distinguishes Game 2 from Game 3 can be used to solve LWE.

Conclusion

Game 0 is the real Basic IBE security game. Game 1 and Game 2 are statistically close to the previous games. Game 2 and Game 3 are computationally indistinguishable under the LWE assumption. In Game 3, the challenge ciphertext is random, so the adversary has zero advantage.

Therefore, Basic IBE is INDr-sID-CPA secure.

This proof only gives selective-ID security because the simulator needs the target identity id∗id^*id∗ before Setup in order to program:

A1=A0R∗−H(id∗)BA_1=A_0R^*-H(id^*)BA1​=A0​R∗−H(id∗)B

Thus, the adversary must commit to id∗id^*id∗ before seeing the public parameters. The Full IBE construction is later introduced to handle adaptive-ID security.

FULL IBE

From Selective to Adaptive-ID (The Intuition)

To upgrade from Selective-ID to Adaptive-ID security, the scheme adopts Waters' hash methodology. Instead of a single matrix A1A_1A1​, the public parameters now contain a sequence of random matrices A1,…,AℓA_1, \dots, A_\ellA1​,…,Aℓ​.

  • An identity is treated as a bit sequence id=(b1,…,bℓ)∈{1,−1}ℓid = (b_1, \dots, b_\ell) \in \{1, -1\}^\ellid=(b1​,…,bℓ​)∈{1,−1}ℓ.
  • The identity matrix is evaluated dynamically as Fid=(A0∣B+∑i=1ℓbiAi)F_{id} = (A_0 \mid B + \sum_{i=1}^\ell b_i A_i)Fid​=(A0​∣B+∑i=1ℓ​bi​Ai​).

The Security Trick: During the security proof, the simulator constructs each Ai=A0Ri+hiBA_i = A_0 R_i + h_i BAi​=A0​Ri​+hi​B (where hi∈Zqh_i \in \mathbb{Z}_qhi​∈Zq​ is a secret coefficient). Expanding this gives:$$F_{id} = \left( A_0 ;\middle|; A_0 \sum_{i=1}^\ell b_i R_i + \left(1 + \sum_{i=1}^\ell b_i h_i\right) B \right)$$ The simulator knows TBT_BTB​ (the trapdoor for $B$).

  • For most queries, 1+∑bihi≠0(modq)1 + \sum b_i h_i \neq 0 \pmod q1+∑bi​hi​=0(modq), allowing the simulator to use TBT_BTB​ to answer key-extraction queries.
  • However, for the target identity id∗id^*id∗ chosen adaptively by the attacker, the term magically cancels out: 1+∑bihi=0(modq)1 + \sum b_i h_i = 0 \pmod q1+∑bi​hi​=0(modq). The BBB matrix disappears from Fid∗F_{id^*}Fid∗​, removing the simulator's ability to extract a key, but perfectly enabling it to embed the LWE challenge ciphertext.

Security Games for Full IBE

Goal of the Proof

Full IBE is proven secure in the adaptive identity model, also called INDr-ID-CPA. Unlike Basic IBE, the adversary does not need to commit to the target identity before setup. It can choose the target identity only later, during the challenge phase.

The proof uses a sequence of games:

Game 0→Game 1→Game 2→Game 3→Game 4\text{Game 0} \rightarrow \text{Game 1} \rightarrow \text{Game 2} \rightarrow \text{Game 3} \rightarrow \text{Game 4}Game 0→Game 1→Game 2→Game 3→Game 4

The goal is to show that a real challenge ciphertext is indistinguishable from a random ciphertext under the LWE assumption.

Game 0: The Real Adaptive-ID Game

Game 0 is the real INDr-ID-CPA game for the Full IBE scheme.

The public parameters are:

PP=(A0,A1,…,Aℓ,B,u)PP=(A_0,A_1,\dots,A_\ell,B,u)PP=(A0​,A1​,…,Aℓ​,B,u)

Here A0A_0A0​ is generated by TrapGen\text{TrapGen}TrapGen, so the challenger knows the trapdoor TA0T_{A_0}TA0​​. The matrices A1,…,Aℓ,BA_1,\dots,A_\ell,BA1​,…,Aℓ​,B are uniformly random.

For an identity:

id=(b1,…,bℓ)∈{1,−1}ℓid=(b_1,\dots,b_\ell)\in\{1,-1\}^{\ell}id=(b1​,…,bℓ​)∈{1,−1}ℓ

define:

Aid=B+∑i=1ℓbiAiA_{id}=B+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} b_iA_iAid​=B+i=1∑ℓ​bi​Ai​

and:

Fid=(A0∣Aid)F_{id}=(A_0 \mid A_{id})Fid​=(A0​∣Aid​)

For private-key queries, the challenger answers using the real extraction algorithm:

e←SampleLeft(A0,Aid,TA0,u,σ)e \leftarrow \text{SampleLeft}(A_0,A_{id},T_{A_0},u,\sigma)e←SampleLeft(A0​,Aid​,TA0​​,u,σ)

where eee satisfies:

Fide=u(modq)F_{id}e=u \pmod qFid​e=u(modq)

Game 1: Programming the Public Matrices

Game 1 changes the way the matrices AiA_iAi​ are generated. The challenger chooses small matrices:

Ri∗←{−1,1}m×mR_i^* \leftarrow \{-1,1\}^{m\times m}Ri∗​←{−1,1}m×m

and random scalars:

hi←Zqh_i \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_qhi​←Zq​

for i=1,…,ℓi=1,\dots,\elli=1,…,ℓ. Using the sign convention of this report, the challenger defines:

Ai=A0Ri∗+hiBA_i=A_0R_i^*+h_iBAi​=A0​Ri∗​+hi​B

This is equivalent to the ABB convention Ai=A0Ri∗−hiBA_i=A_0R_i^*-h_iBAi​=A0​Ri∗​−hi​B after replacing each uniform hih_ihi​ by −hi-h_i−hi​. The important point is that this programming does not require knowing the target identity in advance.

For any identity id=(b1,…,bℓ)id=(b_1,\dots,b_\ell)id=(b1​,…,bℓ​), define:

Rid=∑i=1ℓbiRi∗,hid=1+∑i=1ℓbihi.\begin{aligned} R_{id} &= \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} b_iR_i^*,\\ h_{id} &= 1+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} b_ih_i. \end{aligned}Rid​hid​​=i=1∑ℓ​bi​Ri∗​,=1+i=1∑ℓ​bi​hi​.​

Then:

Aid=B+∑i=1ℓbiAi=B+∑i=1ℓbi(A0Ri∗+hiB)=A0Rid+hidB.\begin{aligned} A_{id} &=B+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}b_iA_i\\ &=B+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}b_i(A_0R_i^*+h_iB)\\ &=A_0R_{id}+h_{id}B. \end{aligned}Aid​​=B+i=1∑ℓ​bi​Ai​=B+i=1∑ℓ​bi​(A0​Ri∗​+hi​B)=A0​Rid​+hid​B.​

Therefore:

Fid=(A0∣A0Rid+hidB)F_{id}=(A_0 \mid A_0R_{id}+h_{id}B)Fid​=(A0​∣A0​Rid​+hid​B)

Game 0 and Game 1 are statistically close because the matrices A0Ri∗A_0R_i^*A0​Ri∗​ look statistically close to uniform. The challenge ciphertext leakage involving (Rid)Ty(R_{id})^Ty(Rid​)Ty is also handled by the same randomness-extraction argument.

Game 2: Adding the Waters Abort Condition

Game 2 adds a hidden abort condition using a Waters-style hash value:

H(id)=hid=1+∑i=1ℓbihiH(id)=h_{id}=1+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}b_ih_iH(id)=hid​=1+i=1∑ℓ​bi​hi​

The simulator wants:

H(id∗)=0H(id^*)=0H(id∗)=0

for the challenge identity, and:

H(idi)≠0H(id_i)\neq 0H(idi​)=0

for every private-key query identity idiid_iidi​.

If this condition fails, the challenger aborts by replacing the adversary's final guess with a fresh random bit. The adversary does not see the hash function and does not know whether an abort happened.

The artificial abort is used to make the non-abort probability almost independent of the adversary's chosen identities. This is the main technical idea from Waters' proof technique.

With this step, the proof loses only a controlled factor in the adversary's advantage:

∣Pr⁡[W2]−12∣≥14q∣Pr⁡[W1]−12∣.\begin{aligned} \left|\Pr[W_2]-\frac{1}{2}\right| &\ge \frac{1}{4q} \left|\Pr[W_1]-\frac{1}{2}\right|. \end{aligned}​Pr[W2​]−21​​​≥4q1​​Pr[W1​]−21​​.​

Game 3: Switching the Trapdoor to BBB

Game 3 changes how A0A_0A0​ and BBB are generated. Now A0A_0A0​ is chosen as a random matrix, while BBB is generated using TrapGen\text{TrapGen}TrapGen. Therefore, the challenger knows the trapdoor TBT_BTB​ instead of TA0T_{A_0}TA0​​.

The matrices AiA_iAi​ are still generated as:

Ai=A0Ri∗+hiBA_i=A_0R_i^*+h_iBAi​=A0​Ri∗​+hi​B

For a private-key query on identity ididid, compute:

Rid=∑i=1ℓbiRi∗,hid=1+∑i=1ℓbihi.\begin{aligned} R_{id} &= \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} b_iR_i^*,\\ h_{id} &= 1+\sum_{i=1}^{\ell} b_ih_i. \end{aligned}Rid​hid​​=i=1∑ℓ​bi​Ri∗​,=1+i=1∑ℓ​bi​hi​.​

Then:

Fid=(A0∣A0Rid+hidB)F_{id}=(A_0 \mid A_0R_{id}+h_{id}B)Fid​=(A0​∣A0​Rid​+hid​B)

If hid=0h_{id}=0hid​=0, the challenger aborts. If hid≠0h_{id}\neq 0hid​=0, then TBT_BTB​ can also be used as a trapdoor for hidBh_{id}Bhid​B, since hidh_{id}hid​ is nonzero in Zq\mathbb{Z}_qZq​.

The challenger answers the key query using:

e←SampleRight(A0,hidB,Rid,TB,u,σ)e \leftarrow \text{SampleRight}(A_0,h_{id}B,R_{id},T_B,u,\sigma)e←SampleRight(A0​,hid​B,Rid​,TB​,u,σ)

The output eee is statistically close to a valid secret key for ididid.

For the target identity id∗id^*id∗, the non-abort condition requires:

hid∗=0h_{id^*}=0hid∗​=0

So:

Fid∗=(A0∣A0Rid∗)F_{id^*}=(A_0 \mid A_0R_{id^*})Fid∗​=(A0​∣A0​Rid∗​)

This form is exactly what is needed to embed the LWE challenge ciphertext. Game 2 and Game 3 are identical from the adversary's view, because the public parameters and private-key answers have the same distributions up to negligible statistical distance.

Game 4: Random Challenge Ciphertext

Game 4 is the same as Game 3, except that the challenge ciphertext is replaced by a uniformly random element of the ciphertext space:

CT∗←Zq×Zq2mCT^* \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_q \times \mathbb{Z}_q^{2m}CT∗←Zq​×Zq2m​

Since the challenge ciphertext is random and independent of the challenge bit, the adversary has zero advantage in this game.

Reduction from LWE

The difference between Game 3 and Game 4 is bounded by the hardness of LWE.

The simulator receives LWE samples:

(ui,vi)(u_i,v_i)(ui​,vi​)

It uses u1,…,umu_1,\dots,u_mu1​,…,um​ to construct:

A0=[u1∣⋯∣um]A_0=[u_1|\cdots|u_m]A0​=[u1​∣⋯∣um​]

and uses u0u_0u0​ as the public vector uuu.

For the challenge ciphertext, let:

v∗=(v1,…,vm)Tv^*=(v_1,\dots,v_m)^Tv∗=(v1​,…,vm​)T

For the target identity id∗=(b1∗,…,bℓ∗)id^*=(b_1^*,\dots,b_\ell^*)id∗=(b1∗​,…,bℓ∗​), define:

Rid∗∗=∑i=1ℓbi∗Ri∗R_{id^*}^*=\sum_{i=1}^{\ell}b_i^*R_i^*Rid∗∗​=i=1∑ℓ​bi∗​Ri∗​

The simulator sets:

c0∗=v0+b∗⌊q2⌋c_0^*=v_0+b^*\left\lfloor\frac{q}{2}\right\rfloorc0∗​=v0​+b∗⌊2q​⌋

and:

c1∗=[v∗(Rid∗∗)Tv∗]c_1^*= \begin{bmatrix} v^*\\ (R_{id^*}^*)^Tv^* \end{bmatrix}c1∗​=[v∗(Rid∗∗​)Tv∗​]

If the oracle is an LWE oracle, then:

v∗=A0Ts+yv^*=A_0^Ts+yv∗=A0T​s+y

Because the non-abort condition gives hid∗=0h_{id^*}=0hid∗​=0, we have:

Fid∗=(A0∣A0Rid∗∗)F_{id^*}=(A_0 \mid A_0R_{id^*}^*)Fid∗​=(A0​∣A0​Rid∗∗​)

Therefore:

c1∗=[A0Ts+y(Rid∗∗)T(A0Ts+y)]=[A0Ts+y(A0Rid∗∗)Ts+(Rid∗∗)Ty]=Fid∗Ts+[y(Rid∗∗)Ty].\begin{aligned} c_1^* &= \begin{bmatrix} A_0^Ts+y\\ (R_{id^*}^*)^T(A_0^Ts+y) \end{bmatrix}\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} A_0^Ts+y\\ (A_0R_{id^*}^*)^Ts+(R_{id^*}^*)^Ty \end{bmatrix}\\ &= F_{id^*}^Ts+ \begin{bmatrix} y\\ (R_{id^*}^*)^Ty \end{bmatrix}. \end{aligned}c1∗​​=[A0T​s+y(Rid∗∗​)T(A0T​s+y)​]=[A0T​s+y(A0​Rid∗∗​)Ts+(Rid∗∗​)Ty​]=Fid∗T​s+[y(Rid∗∗​)Ty​].​

This is exactly the c1c_1c1​ part of a real challenge ciphertext in Game 3. Also, since v0=uTs+xv_0=u^Ts+xv0​=uTs+x, we have:

c0∗=uTs+x+b∗⌊q2⌋c_0^*=u^Ts+x+b^*\left\lfloor\frac{q}{2}\right\rfloorc0∗​=uTs+x+b∗⌊2q​⌋

which matches the real encryption form.

If the oracle is random, then v0v_0v0​ and v∗v^*v∗ are uniform random. By the leftover hash lemma, the whole challenge ciphertext is statistically close to uniform, as in Game 4.

Therefore, any adversary that distinguishes Game 3 from Game 4 can be used to solve LWE.

Conclusion

  • Game 0 is the real adaptive-ID security game.
  • Game 1 is statistically close to Game 0.
  • Game 2 adds a hidden Waters abort condition and loses only a controlled factor.
  • Game 3 switches the trapdoor from A0A_0A0​ to BBB without changing the adversary's view.
  • Game 4 replaces the challenge ciphertext with a random ciphertext.
  • Game 3 and Game 4 are computationally indistinguishable under the LWE assumption.
  • In Game 4, the adversary has zero advantage.

Thus:

∣Pr⁡[W0]−12∣≤4q⋅LWE-adv[B].\begin{aligned} \left|\Pr[W_0]-\frac{1}{2}\right| &\le 4q\cdot \text{LWE-adv}[\mathcal{B}]. \end{aligned}​Pr[W0​]−21​​​≤4q⋅LWE-adv[B].​

Full IBE achieves adaptive-ID security because the simulator does not need to know the target identity during setup. Instead, it programs all matrices AiA_iAi​ using random coefficients hih_ihi​, and later the Waters hash condition selects identities with H(id)=0H(id)=0H(id)=0. This replaces the Basic IBE trick, where the simulator had to hard-code id∗id^*id∗ directly into A1A_1A1​ before setup.

Hierarchical IBE Construction

From IBE to HIBE: The Intuition

In HIBE, an identity is no longer a single value. Instead, it is a vector:

id=(id1,…,idℓ)id = (id_1,\dots,id_\ell)id=(id1​,…,idℓ​)

where each component satisfies:

idi∈Zqn∖{0}id_i \in \mathbb{Z}_q^n \setminus \{0\}idi​∈Zqn​∖{0}

The value ℓ\ellℓ is the depth of the identity, and the system supports identities up to maximum depth ddd.

For an identity at depth ℓ\ellℓ, define the matrix:

Fid=(A0∣A1+H(id1)B∣⋯∣Aℓ+H(idℓ)B)∈Zqn×(ℓ+1)mF_{id} = \left( A_0 \mid A_1 + H(id_1)B \mid \cdots \mid A_\ell + H(id_\ell)B \right) \in \mathbb{Z}_q^{n \times (\ell+1)m}Fid​=(A0​∣A1​+H(id1​)B∣⋯∣Aℓ​+H(idℓ​)B)∈Zqn×(ℓ+1)m​

The main difference from Basic IBE is the private key format.

  • In Basic IBE, the secret key is a short vector eee such that:
Fide=u(modq)F_{id}e = u \pmod qFid​e=u(modq)
  • In HIBE, the secret key is a short basis for the lattice:
Λq⊥(Fid)\Lambda_q^\bot(F_{id})Λq⊥​(Fid​)

This basis allows the user to delegate keys to children identities.

1. Setup

  • Input: Security parameter λ\lambdaλ and maximum hierarchy depth ddd.
  • Parameters: Set q,n,m,σˉ,αˉq,n,m,\bar{\sigma},\bar{\alpha}q,n,m,σˉ,αˉ, where:
σˉ=(σ1,…,σd)\bar{\sigma} = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_d)σˉ=(σ1​,…,σd​)

and

αˉ=(α1,…,αd)\bar{\alpha} = (\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_d)αˉ=(α1​,…,αd​)
  • Generate Root Matrix: Run:
TrapGen(q,n)\text{TrapGen}(q,n)TrapGen(q,n)

to obtain a uniformly random matrix:

A0∈Zqn×mA_0 \in \mathbb{Z}_q^{n \times m}A0​∈Zqn×m​

and a short trapdoor basis:

TA0 for Λq⊥(A0)T_{A_0} \text{ for } \Lambda_q^\bot(A_0)TA0​​ for Λq⊥​(A0​)
  • Generate Random Matrices: Select:
A1,…,Ad,B←Zqn×mA_1,\dots,A_d,B \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_q^{n \times m}A1​,…,Ad​,B←Zqn×m​

uniformly at random.

  • Generate Random Vector: Select:
u←Zqnu \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_q^nu←Zqn​

PP=(A0,A1,…,Ad,B,u)PP = (A_0,A_1,\dots,A_d,B,u)PP=(A0​,A1​,…,Ad​,B,u)

and

MK=TA0MK = T_{A_0}MK=TA0​​

2. Derive

The Derive algorithm allows a parent identity to generate the secret key for its child.

Let the parent identity be:

id=(id1,…,idℓ−1)id = (id_1,\dots,id_{\ell-1})id=(id1​,…,idℓ−1​)

and the child identity be:

id′=(id1,…,idℓ−1,idℓ)id' = (id_1,\dots,id_{\ell-1},id_\ell)id′=(id1​,…,idℓ−1​,idℓ​)

Assume the parent already has a secret key:

SKidSK_{id}SKid​

where SKidSK_{id}SKid​ is a short basis for:

Λq⊥(Fid)\Lambda_q^\bot(F_{id})Λq⊥​(Fid​)

The child matrix is:

Fid′=(Fid∣Aℓ+H(idℓ)B)F_{id'} = \left( F_{id} \mid A_\ell + H(id_\ell)B \right)Fid′​=(Fid​∣Aℓ​+H(idℓ​)B)

SKid′←SampleBasisLeft(Fid,Aℓ+H(idℓ)B,SKid,σℓ)SK_{id'} \leftarrow \text{SampleBasisLeft} \left( F_{id}, A_\ell + H(id_\ell)B, SK_{id}, \sigma_\ell \right)SKid′​←SampleBasisLeft(Fid​,Aℓ​+H(idℓ​)B,SKid​,σℓ​)

Λq⊥(Fid′)\Lambda_q^\bot(F_{id'})Λq⊥​(Fid′​)

3. Extract

The Extract algorithm is just a special case of Derive from the root.

For the empty identity ε\varepsilonε, define:

Fε=A0F_{\varepsilon} = A_0Fε​=A0​

id=(id1,…,idℓ)id = (id_1,\dots,id_\ell)id=(id1​,…,idℓ​)

where SKidSK_{id}SKid​ is a short basis for:

Key Difference from Basic IBE

In Basic IBE, the private key is directly a short vector:

esuch thatFide=u(modq)e \quad\text{such that}\quad F_{id}e = u \pmod qesuch thatFid​e=u(modq)

In HIBE, the private key is a short basis:

SKidforΛq⊥(Fid)SK_{id} \quad\text{for}\quad \Lambda_q^\bot(F_{id})SKid​forΛq⊥​(Fid​)

This basis can be used for two purposes:

  1. To decrypt, by sampling a short preimage:
eid←SamplePre(Fid,SKid,u,τℓ)e_{id} \leftarrow \text{SamplePre}(F_{id},SK_{id},u,\tau_\ell)eid​←SamplePre(Fid​,SKid​,u,τℓ​)
  1. To delegate child keys using:
SampleBasisLeft\text{SampleBasisLeft}SampleBasisLeft

Therefore, HIBE supports hierarchical key delegation while keeping the same LWE-based encryption structure.

Security Games for HIBE

Goal of the Proof

The HIBE construction is proven secure in the selective identity model, also called INDr-sID-CPA.

In this game, the adversary must declare the target identity before setup:

id∗=(id1∗,…,idk∗)id^* = (id_1^*, \dots, id_k^*)id∗=(id1∗​,…,idk∗​)

where k≤dk \le dk≤d.

The proof uses a sequence of games:

Game 0→Game 1→Game 2→Game 3\text{Game 0} \rightarrow \text{Game 1} \rightarrow \text{Game 2} \rightarrow \text{Game 3}Game 0→Game 1→Game 2→Game 3

The goal is to show that a valid challenge ciphertext is indistinguishable from a random ciphertext under the LWE assumption.

Game 0: The Real HIBE Game

Game 0 is the real INDr-sID-CPA game for the HIBE scheme.

The challenger generates:

PP=(A0,A1,…,Ad,B,u)PP = (A_0,A_1,\dots,A_d,B,u)PP=(A0​,A1​,…,Ad​,B,u)

where A0A_0A0​ is generated by TrapGen\text{TrapGen}TrapGen, so the challenger knows:

TA0 for Λq⊥(A0)T_{A_0} \text{ for } \Lambda_q^\bot(A_0)TA0​​ for Λq⊥​(A0​)

For an identity:

id=(id1,…,idℓ)id = (id_1,\dots,id_\ell)id=(id1​,…,idℓ​)

define:

Fid=(A0∣A1+H(id1)B∣⋯∣Aℓ+H(idℓ)B)F_{id} = \left( A_0 \mid A_1 + H(id_1)B \mid \cdots \mid A_\ell + H(id_\ell)B \right)Fid​=(A0​∣A1​+H(id1​)B∣⋯∣Aℓ​+H(idℓ​)B)

Private-key queries are answered using the real extraction and delegation algorithms. The output is a short basis:

SKid for Λq⊥(Fid)SK_{id} \text{ for } \Lambda_q^\bot(F_{id})SKid​ for Λq⊥​(Fid​)

The adversary is not allowed to query any identity that is a prefix of the target identity id∗id^*id∗.

Game 1: Programming the Public Matrices

Game 1 changes the way the matrices A1,…,AdA_1,\dots,A_dA1​,…,Ad​ are generated.

Let the target identity be:

id∗=(id1∗,…,idk∗)id^*=(id_1^*,\dots,id_k^*)id∗=(id1∗​,…,idk∗​)

If k<dk<dk<d, pad it with zeros until depth ddd:

id∗=(id1∗,…,idk∗,0,…,0)id^*=(id_1^*,\dots,id_k^*,0,\dots,0)id∗=(id1∗​,…,idk∗​,0,…,0)

The challenger chooses random matrices:

R1∗,…,Rd∗←{−1,1}m×mR_1^*,\dots,R_d^* \leftarrow \{-1,1\}^{m\times m}R1∗​,…,Rd∗​←{−1,1}m×m

and defines:

Ai=A0Ri∗−H(idi∗)BA_i = A_0R_i^* - H(id_i^*)BAi​=A0​Ri∗​−H(idi∗​)B

for every i=1,…,di=1,\dots,di=1,…,d.

For an identity id=(id1,…,idℓ)id=(id_1,\dots,id_\ell)id=(id1​,…,idℓ​), we get:

Fid=(A0∣A1+H(id1)B∣⋯∣Aℓ+H(idℓ)B)=(A0∣A0R1∗+(H(id1)−H(id1∗))B∣⋯∣A0Rℓ∗+(H(idℓ)−H(idℓ∗))B)\begin{aligned} F_{id} &= \left( A_0 \mid A_1 + H(id_1)B \mid \cdots \mid A_\ell + H(id_\ell)B \right)\\ &= \left( A_0 \mid A_0R_1^* + (H(id_1)-H(id_1^*))B \mid \cdots \mid A_0R_\ell^* + (H(id_\ell)-H(id_\ell^*))B \right) \end{aligned}Fid​​=(A0​∣A1​+H(id1​)B∣⋯∣Aℓ​+H(idℓ​)B)=(A0​∣A0​R1∗​+(H(id1​)−H(id1∗​))B∣⋯∣A0​Rℓ∗​+(H(idℓ​)−H(idℓ∗​))B)​

Define:

R‾ℓ∗=(R1∗∣⋯∣Rℓ∗)∈Zqm×ℓm\overline{R}_\ell^* = (R_1^* \mid \cdots \mid R_\ell^*) \in \mathbb{Z}_q^{m\times \ell m}Rℓ∗​=(R1∗​∣⋯∣Rℓ∗​)∈Zqm×ℓm​

and:

Bid=((H(id1)−H(id1∗))B∣⋯∣(H(idℓ)−H(idℓ∗))B)B_{id} = \left( (H(id_1)-H(id_1^*))B \mid \cdots \mid (H(id_\ell)-H(id_\ell^*))B \right)Bid​=((H(id1​)−H(id1∗​))B∣⋯∣(H(idℓ​)−H(idℓ∗​))B)

Then:

Fid=(A0∣A0R‾ℓ∗+Bid)F_{id} = \left( A_0 \mid A_0\overline{R}_\ell^* + B_{id} \right)Fid​=(A0​∣A0​Rℓ∗​+Bid​)

In the challenge phase, for the target identity at depth kkk, we have:

Fid∗=(A0∣A0R‾k∗)F_{id^*} = \left( A_0 \mid A_0\overline{R}_k^* \right)Fid∗​=(A0​∣A0​Rk∗​)

because:

H(idi∗)−H(idi∗)=0H(id_i^*) - H(id_i^*) = 0H(idi∗​)−H(idi∗​)=0

Game 0 and Game 1 are statistically indistinguishable by the leftover hash lemma. The matrices A0Ri∗A_0R_i^*A0​Ri∗​ look statistically close to uniform, so the public matrices AiA_iAi​ still look random to the adversary.

Game 2: Switching the Trapdoor to BBB

Game 2 changes how A0A_0A0​ and BBB are generated.

  • A0A_0A0​ is chosen uniformly at random.
  • BBB is generated using TrapGen\text{TrapGen}TrapGen.

So the challenger now knows:

TB for Λq⊥(B)T_B \text{ for } \Lambda_q^\bot(B)TB​ for Λq⊥​(B)

instead of knowing a trapdoor for A0A_0A0​.

The matrices AiA_iAi​ are still programmed as:

Ai=A0Ri∗−H(idi∗)BA_i = A_0R_i^* - H(id_i^*)BAi​=A0​Ri∗​−H(idi∗​)B

Now consider a private-key query for:

id=(id1,…,idℓ)id=(id_1,\dots,id_\ell)id=(id1​,…,idℓ​)

where ididid is not a prefix of id∗id^*id∗.

The challenger must output a short basis for:

Λq⊥(Fid)\Lambda_q^\bot(F_{id})Λq⊥​(Fid​)

where:

Fid=(A0∣A0R‾ℓ∗+Bid)F_{id} = \left( A_0 \mid A_0\overline{R}_\ell^* + B_{id} \right)Fid​=(A0​∣A0​Rℓ∗​+Bid​)

Because ididid is not a prefix of id∗id^*id∗, there exists some index jjj such that:

idj≠idj∗id_j \neq id_j^*idj​=idj∗​

Since HHH is an FRD encoding, we know:

H(idj)−H(idj∗)H(id_j)-H(id_j^*)H(idj​)−H(idj∗​)

is full rank.

Therefore, BidB_{id}Bid​ has rank nnn whenever BBB has rank nnn. This allows the simulator to use the trapdoor TBT_BTB​ to build a short basis for Λq⊥(Bid)\Lambda_q^\bot(B_{id})Λq⊥​(Bid​), and then apply SampleBasisRight.

The challenger answers the query by running:

SKid←SampleBasisRight(A0,Bid,R‾ℓ∗,TB,σℓ)SK_{id} \leftarrow \text{SampleBasisRight} ( A_0, B_{id}, \overline{R}_\ell^*, T_B, \sigma_\ell )SKid​←SampleBasisRight(A0​,Bid​,Rℓ∗​,TB​,σℓ​)

The output is a short basis for:

Λq⊥(Fid)\Lambda_q^\bot(F_{id})Λq⊥​(Fid​)

and its distribution is statistically close to the real key distribution from Game 1.

Thus, Game 1 and Game 2 are statistically indistinguishable.

Game 3: Random Challenge Ciphertext

Game 3 is identical to Game 2, except the challenge ciphertext is replaced by a uniformly random element:

CT∗←Zq×Zqm+kmCT^* \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_q \times \mathbb{Z}_q^{m+km}CT∗←Zq​×Zqm+km​

Since the ciphertext is completely random and independent of the challenge bit, the adversary has zero advantage in Game 3.

It remains to show that Game 2 and Game 3 are computationally indistinguishable. This is done by a reduction from LWE.

Reduction from LWE

Assume there exists an adversary that distinguishes Game 2 from Game 3 with non-negligible advantage. We build an algorithm B\mathcal{B}B that solves LWE.

The LWE oracle gives samples:

(ui,vi)∈Zqn×Zq(u_i,v_i)\in \mathbb{Z}_q^n \times \mathbb{Z}_q(ui​,vi​)∈Zqn​×Zq​

for i=0,…,mi=0,\dots,mi=0,…,m.

The oracle is either:

  • a real LWE oracle:
vi=uiTs+xiv_i = u_i^Ts + x_ivi​=uiT​s+xi​

for some secret s∈Zqns\in \mathbb{Z}_q^ns∈Zqn​ and noise xix_ixi​,

  • or a uniform random oracle.

Setup of the Reduction

The simulator constructs:

A0=[u1∣⋯∣um]A_0 = [u_1 \mid \cdots \mid u_m]A0​=[u1​∣⋯∣um​]

and uses u0u_0u0​ as the public vector:

u=u0u = u_0u=u0​

It then constructs B,A1,…,AdB,A_1,\dots,A_dB,A1​,…,Ad​ as in Game 2:

Ai=A0Ri∗−H(idi∗)BA_i = A_0R_i^* - H(id_i^*)BAi​=A0​Ri∗​−H(idi∗​)B

The public parameters are:

PP=(A0,A1,…,Ad,B,u)PP=(A_0,A_1,\dots,A_d,B,u)PP=(A0​,A1​,…,Ad​,B,u)

Private-key queries are answered exactly as in Game 2 using SampleBasisRight.

Challenge Ciphertext

Let:

v∗=[v1⋮vm]∈Zqmv^* = \begin{bmatrix} v_1\\ \vdots\\ v_m \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{Z}_q^mv∗=​v1​⋮vm​​​∈Zqm​

For the target identity:

id∗=(id1∗,…,idk∗)id^*=(id_1^*,\dots,id_k^*)id∗=(id1∗​,…,idk∗​)

define:

R‾k∗=(R1∗∣⋯∣Rk∗)\overline{R}_k^* = (R_1^* \mid \cdots \mid R_k^*)Rk∗​=(R1∗​∣⋯∣Rk∗​)

The simulator sets:

c0∗=v0+b∗⌊q2⌋c_0^* = v_0 + b^*\left\lfloor \frac q2 \right\rfloorc0∗​=v0​+b∗⌊2q​⌋

and:

c1∗=[v∗(R‾k∗)Tv∗]c_1^* = \begin{bmatrix} v^*\\ (\overline{R}_k^*)^T v^* \end{bmatrix}c1∗​=[v∗(Rk∗​)Tv∗​]

Then:

CT∗=(c0∗,c1∗)CT^*=(c_0^*,c_1^*)CT∗=(c0∗​,c1∗​)

When the Oracle is LWE

If the oracle is an LWE oracle, then:

v∗=A0Ts+yv^* = A_0^Ts + yv∗=A0T​s+y

where:

y←Ψˉαkmy \leftarrow \bar{\Psi}_{\alpha_k}^my←Ψˉαk​m​

Also:

v0=uTs+xv_0 = u^Ts + xv0​=uTs+x

For the target identity, the programmed matrix satisfies:

Fid∗=(A0∣A0R‾k∗)F_{id^*} = \left( A_0 \mid A_0\overline{R}_k^* \right)Fid∗​=(A0​∣A0​Rk∗​)

Therefore:

c1∗=[v∗(R‾k∗)Tv∗]=[A0Ts+y(R‾k∗)T(A0Ts+y)]=[A0Ts+y(A0R‾k∗)Ts+(R‾k∗)Ty]=Fid∗Ts+[y(R‾k∗)Ty]\begin{aligned} c_1^* &= \begin{bmatrix} v^*\\ (\overline{R}_k^*)^Tv^* \end{bmatrix}\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} A_0^Ts+y\\ (\overline{R}_k^*)^T(A_0^Ts+y) \end{bmatrix}\\ &= \begin{bmatrix} A_0^Ts+y\\ (A_0\overline{R}_k^*)^Ts+(\overline{R}_k^*)^Ty \end{bmatrix}\\ &= F_{id^*}^Ts + \begin{bmatrix} y\\ (\overline{R}_k^*)^Ty \end{bmatrix} \end{aligned}c1∗​​=[v∗(Rk∗​)Tv∗​]=[A0T​s+y(Rk∗​)T(A0T​s+y)​]=[A0T​s+y(A0​Rk∗​)Ts+(Rk∗​)Ty​]=Fid∗T​s+[y(Rk∗​)Ty​]​

This is exactly the c1c_1c1​ part of a valid HIBE ciphertext.

Also:

c0∗=uTs+x+b∗⌊q2⌋c_0^* = u^Ts+x+b^*\left\lfloor\frac q2\right\rfloorc0∗​=uTs+x+b∗⌊2q​⌋

which is exactly the c0c_0c0​ part of a valid encryption.

So when the oracle is LWE, the adversary sees Game 2.

When the Oracle is Random

If the oracle is random, then:

v0←Zqv_0 \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_qv0​←Zq​

and:

v∗←Zqmv^* \leftarrow \mathbb{Z}_q^mv∗←Zqm​

are uniformly random.

By the leftover hash lemma, the vector:

[v∗(R‾k∗)Tv∗]\begin{bmatrix} v^*\\ (\overline{R}_k^*)^Tv^* \end{bmatrix}[v∗(Rk∗​)Tv∗​]

is statistically close to uniform in:

Zqm+km\mathbb{Z}_q^{m+km}Zqm+km​

Therefore, the challenge ciphertext is a uniformly random element of:

Zq×Zqm+km\mathbb{Z}_q \times \mathbb{Z}_q^{m+km}Zq​×Zqm+km​

So when the oracle is random, the adversary sees Game 3.

Conclusion

If an adversary can distinguish Game 2 from Game 3, then the simulator can distinguish LWE samples from random samples.

Thus:

Game 2≈cGame 3\text{Game 2} \approx_c \text{Game 3}Game 2≈c​Game 3

under the LWE assumption.

Combining all games:

Game 0≈sGame 1\text{Game 0} \approx_s \text{Game 1}Game 0≈s​Game 1 Game 1≈sGame 2\text{Game 1} \approx_s \text{Game 2}Game 1≈s​Game 2 Game 2≈cGame 3\text{Game 2} \approx_c \text{Game 3}Game 2≈c​Game 3

In Game 3, the challenge ciphertext is random, so the adversary has zero advantage.

Therefore, the HIBE construction is INDr-sID-CPA secure under the LWE assumption.
